realRuntimeExemptions.reason: AB-278's ratified Decision (2026-09-03) names this module as "the one module allowed to call the real globals because it is their injection point": createDefaultRuntimeServices() is the sole real-globals implementation of the RuntimeServices contract (AB-252). Every other module composes against the RuntimeServices interface and swaps in createManualRuntimeServices() for tests instead.

This is the direct test of createDefaultRuntimeServices() itself (the real-globals implementation) — it asserts clock.now() tracks the real Date.now(), monotonic.now() tracks real elapsed time, and timers schedule and cancel real callbacks. Injecting createManualRuntimeServices() here would test the fake instead of the real adapter it exists to prove correct.

One assertion ("never calls a real timer — advance() settles synchronously with respect to wall-clock time") measures real performance.now() before and after a 60-second virtual advance() to prove the manual runtime's advance() does not consume real wall-clock time. Proving the absence of a real timer necessarily requires measuring against the real clock as ground truth; an injected manual clock cannot serve as its own control.

AB-98's real-runtime conformance tier (AB-92's test-tier matrix): a real Bun HTTP/SSE/WebSocket loopback server bound to an operating-system-assigned ephemeral port, real fetch/WebSocket clients, and one deterministic bounded-drain read after a duplicate-subscription assertion (AbortSignal/ping-pong fenced, not a fixed sleep) — this tier exists specifically to exercise real sockets, which the deterministic tiers below it cannot.

Svelte hook tests assign globalThis.fetch/WebSocket/EventSource directly to install fakes (5 files: use-chat, use-reviews, use-run-detail, use-runs, use-websocket .svelte.test.ts). AB-273 injects fetch/WebSocket/EventSource/timers through a client environment so these tests stop mutating process globals.

Names a Bun.build glue entry temp file with crypto.randomUUID() so two concurrent agent-validation processes bundling the real Durable Object worker at once never write/read/race-delete the same file. No caller-injected options.identifiers value is safe here: a caller's identifier source is not guaranteed process-unique (test/cloudflare-backend-contract.test.ts uses a plain per-process counter), and this module ships as part of src/ (tsconfig.build.json rootDir is ./src), so it cannot import a default from outside src/test/ the way the *.test.ts files (excluded from the build) do.

waitForRunCompletion's terminal-status poll needs a real per-iteration setTimeout delay, not the zero-delay MessageChannel macrotask loop waitForCondition (operative/test) and the rest of this codebase's polling uses. Measured directly against the new lmdb storage fixture (AB-261): a 5,000-iteration zero-delay macrotask spin (~600ms of real time) left two concurrently-running LMDB-backed runs still 'running', while the identical scenario polled with a real setTimeout(5) between checks completed both well within a couple hundred milliseconds. A tight macrotask-only loop evidently starves the lmdb native library's own async completion callbacks rather than merely running out of iterations, so more zero-delay attempts does not fix it — only letting real wall-clock time elapse between checks does. Still a bounded, condition-checked poll (asserts the observed run status every iteration, fails loudly past its cap), never a fixed-duration sleep standing in for a real check.
